references.text: Philip finds Nathanael and passes on the same message: "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote" (John 1:45). The same pattern of finding someone and proclaiming the Messiah.

The Samaritan woman expresses her expectation of the Messiah: "I know that the Messiah is coming" (John 4:25). Both here and in John 1:41, the Hebrew word "Messiah" is used with an explanation that it means "Christ."
The Samaritan woman invites others to come and see him who may be the Messiah (John 4:29), just as Andrew brings his brother Simon to Jesus.

Daniel's prophecy about the "anointed one" (Messiah) who is to come (Daniel 9:25-26). This is one of the most important Old Testament texts that uses the title "Messiah" (the anointed one) directly, and to which Andrew's confession points back.
Andrew was one of the two disciples who first followed Jesus after John the Baptist's testimony (John 1:35-37). It was this meeting that led him to go and find his brother Simon.
Matthew's account of the calling of Simon and Andrew (Matthew 4:18-20). Andrew and Simon Peter are brothers, and in all the Gospels they are linked together in following Jesus.

Peter's great confession: "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). Andrew brought Simon to Jesus with the message "We have found the Messiah," and later Peter himself confesses Jesus as the Messiah.
The psalm speaks of the Lord's anointed (Messiah/Christ): "against the Lord and his anointed" (Psalm 2:2). The Old Testament expectation of the anointed king that Andrew confesses to have found.

"The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me" (Isaiah 61:1). The prophecy of the anointed one (Messiah) who is sent to proclaim good news—the anointed one whom Andrew declares he has found.

Jesus gives Simon the new name Cephas (Peter) when Andrew brings him (John 1:42). This is the direct continuation of Andrew's confession of Jesus as Messiah and shows the consequence of having found the Messiah.
